facts.statement: The main experiment evaluated a reliability-weighted planning algorithm on 1,800 runs across six deterministic 8x8 mazes with varying levels of model error.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The reliability-weighted method and a standard model-free learning approach both achieved perfect success rates when only the planning model was corrupted, whereas unweighted planning methods performed worse.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: On larger grids, the reliability-aware method's success rate dropped from 100% to 60% as corruption increased, while the model-free method failed completely in greedy evaluation within a 200-episode limit.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: A follow-up test showed that the model-free method's success rate improved to 77.5% at 500 episodes and reached 100% at 1,000 episodes, indicating the earlier failure was due to limited training time.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The authors conclude that the model-free method's poor performance was a result of insufficient training episodes rather than an inherent inability to solve those specific maps.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: In environments with random action errors, the reliability-weighted method was more resilient to model corruption but performed worse than a fixed planning method when no corruption was present.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: Simplified versions of three intrinsic-exploration algorithms were unable to solve a 16x16 maze within a 200-episode limit.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The connection to hippocampal replay is presented as a computational analogy rather than a claim about actual neural mechanisms.
facts.subject: computational
